en: Regarding the *Vajraśekhara-sūtra: The Ritual Manual of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣarāja*, here is the phonetic commentary on the text from "I bow my head" up to "therefore I constantly take refuge. The praise says:
Of these eight verses, the first five lines contain five [points]. That is to say, in the first line, the term "Samantabhadra" refers to the Principle (tattva). Namely—
This is because the single character subsumes all the Buddhas mentioned below;
alternatively, it may be divided into two Buddhas,
namely Samantabhadra and the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) of the Buddhas.
Alternatively, they may be divided into three Buddhas,
which consists of the previous two plus the one who has realized great enlightenment through direct manifestation (*abhisambuddha*).
Alternatively, they may be divided into four wisdoms (*jñāna*).
That is to say, Samantabhadra is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, which is Akṣobhya Buddha;
the next line, the Wondrous Observational Wisdom, is Amitābha Buddha;
and the next line, the Wisdom of Equality, is Ratnasambhava Buddha.
The single phrase "the wheel of the transformative teaching" refers to the Wisdom of Accomplishing Activities, which is the Buddha Amoghasiddhi.
Alternatively, it may be divided into five wisdoms by adding the Wisdom of the Essential Nature of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-svabhāva-jñāna) to the preceding four.
That which is called "Receiving the Name" refers to the single phrase "Vajradhātu.
From this point downward, the subsequent phrases are assigned to the four directions as well as the central Womb [maṇḍala] of Vairocana Buddha.
These flow forth from the crown of one's own head.
The two lines beginning with "Great Vajra Vidyārāja" refer to the Buddha of the East.
The two lines beginning with "Majestic Radiance" refer to the Buddha of the South.
The two lines beginning with "For the Sake of All" refer to the Buddha of the West.
From their initial manifestation until their passing, they all belong to the Northern Buddha;
because they reach the single essence, they are the Buddhas of the Central Essence.
The subsequent two lines refer to the Eastern Buddha.
The next two phrases refer to the Buddha of the South.
The next two phrases refer to the Buddha of the West.
The next two [phrases] refer to the Buddha of the Central Body.
The Buddha who has attained enlightenment and is equal to space is the Buddha of the North.
Next is one Buddha of the Essential Body.
Next are two Buddhas of the East.
Next, the two western Buddhas cause one to recite the single phrase "Nan-butsu" (Homage to the Buddha) all at once;
therefore, one should always take refuge in the single northern Buddha.
Now, I shall separately explain the phonetics and meanings of the characters in the text.
"Shuo" (爍) is pronounced as "shi" (釋); "he" (河) means "river" (河); "ji" (飢) is pronounced as "xu" (須); "liu" (留) means "to cause" (令);
and "shan" (善) means "good" (善).
Therefore, it is the reality:
one should select fine cloth to make the *zuan* garment;
"jiǎn" (揀) is pronounced kě'ěr fǎn.

"Clan" (*jùxìng*) refers to the four castes (*sìxìng*). "Qi-jì" (pronounced *yīfǎn*): *nǎi* [is followed by] *liú*, *mò* [is pronounced with the] *pó* [rhyme], and *chuān* [is] *wànjǐ*. *Tài* [is] *jiǔ*. (Note:
This appears to be a glossary entry or phonetic commentary on the characters for "clan," "four castes," and other related terms, likely from a medieval Chinese lexicographical or exegetical work.)
*Gěi* (pronounced *xǔ* with a retroflex *r*) is the name of a plant; *hūn* (pronounced *guǐ* with a retroflex *r*) is the name of a ghost;
*dí* (pronounced *zhì* with an affricate *yì*) is the name of a place; *zhǐ* (pronounced *liáng*) is the name of a person; *jiā* is the name of a person; *xū* is the name of a person.

*Maṇḍala*: In the Sanskrit language, this is translated as "altar" (*tán*). It is written with the characters 磨須留拭 (pronounced *ma-xu-liu-shi*, with the second character read as *zhì-yì-fǎn*) and 川波久 (pronounced *chuān-bō-jǐu*).
*Maṇḍala* is the Sanskrit term; in this context, it refers to a ritual platform.
*Pei* (pronounced *pe*) and *bo* (pronounced *yī*) are reversed; *chuān* is *yú*;
*bùmáo* is *bùjiǔ*;
*wúyú* is the Sanskrit term, which in this [Chinese] context is translated as "correspondence" (*yoga*).
Huá guǒ hé fǎn nài tài liáng ěr cè zǔ pō wú yā yú xū.
Feng (鋒): sharp and pointed; upper radical *zhǐ* (止), lower radical *jiā* (加). Lì (銳): pointed; upper radical *zhǐ* (止), lower radical *zhì* (志). Sù (素): white;
upper radical *yuè* (月), lower radical *bái* (白). Mǔ (拇): thumb; upper radical *bǎo* (保), lower radical *yóu* (由). Bǐ (比): compare; upper radical *bǎo* (保), lower radical *bǐ* (比).
Zhuo-ze-zuo-bu-ke-neng-ye-e-bi-tai-bi-yin-jia-jiu-fan.
The left arm is spread out;
the legs are spread out with their hairs standing on end;
behind the head is *chinnanaku*.
Ūru-roma-vikīrṇa-jānu-bhitti-samantāt.
"Mei kou ye siddhi" (美口也悉地) means "accomplishment" (成就);
"san zuo er fan chuan jia zuo" (繖左爾反川加左) is the phonetic transcription.

*Chánjuān*: the first character is pronounced *shàn* (with a retroflex -n ending), the second is pronounced *juān* (with a retroflex -n ending); it means "excessive" (*tài hū yě*) and "to add" (*jiā nà liú zhuàng yě*).
*Jù*: "extreme" (*shèn yě*).
*Tiáo*: "to harmonize the will" (*zhì liáng bù*).
The practitioner is like the cessation of cessation;
it is subtle and non-existent,
harmonious and added, yet without a master.
"De qiǎo yóu yóu" (搯取也由猶) means "to seize and hold fast";
"yuān wàn fǎn ā tài" (冤蒬反阿太) is the phonetic transcription of the sound.
Morning: Ajita;
noon: Vāyu; evening: Yūbu.
Mubuyuhujinmaojiangjiubiqiaawanzijiu.
Chin-nyo ku-so a-nae ku-ryu kan-sa ga-bu.
Tiān (䐡) is pronounced as *bǎo* (保); zǔ (祖) is pronounced as *fú* (馝), with the rhyme category *bǐ* (鄙); liè (列) has the same rhyme;
fù (馞) is pronounced as *bó* (馞), with the rhyme category *mò* (沒).
The Master, Kawa Ikezane,
built this Cloud Terrace (Unkai) on a high mound of earth.
The pavilion was constructed of wood and raised high;
its form and attire were identical to those of the Patriarch. One by one, they proceeded toward the hall, having already purified both body and speech.
Upon entering the chamber, assume the seated posture.
Perform the three secret mudrās: three times with the hand marked by the syllable *aṃ*, three times with the tongue, and three times with the mind.
Having completed these recitations, next purify the body and the site with the syllable *raṃ*, burning them both completely clean.
Next, perform the heart mudrā of the Buddha Family at the crown of the head and recite three times.
Next, place the heart mudrā of the Lotus Family upon the right thumb and recite three times near the right ear.
Next, place the left thumb of the Vajra-family heart-mudrā against the left ear and recite three times. Then,
perform the consecration with the Aparājita mudrā.
Thereafter, perform the ritual for entering the hall;
that is, contemplate: "I am Vajrasattva," and so forth.
Then enter the hall.
Having performed the prostrations to the Buddha, the offering of incense, and the application of unguents,
and having completed the mudrās of the three families.

Next, perform the seal and recite the words for the universal prostration while standing on the right foot, saying "I take refuge," etc. [Recite] the contemplation of the four immeasurables; the words and seal of bodhicitta; the words and seal of the invincible protection-knot; the contemplation of the three liberations; the contemplation of the five signs; the root mantra and seal of the deity—also known as the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa Cakra Mantra; the three-syllable mantra of Vairocana—also known as the Body-Mantra; the words and seal of empowerment; the words and seal of offering; the seal of praise; the offering of arghya; the words and seal of Buddhalocanā. Furthermore, regarding the root mantra of Jñānamuṣṭi, this refers to the Uṣṇīṣa Seal; by adding this to the aforementioned, one forms the Body Seal. Nevertheless, first perform the root mantra seal. Contemplate the deity and their retinue, each marked with two seals at the four locations. Perform the mantra-seal of the rosary; once the count of recitations is complete, next perform the empowerment seal of the root mantra at the four locations.
Furthermore, apply the seal of the body (*kāyamudrā*).
Then, forming the seal of meditative concentration (*samādhimudrā*), enter into contemplation;
contemplate the meaning of the syllable, the lunar disc, the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and so forth.

Having emerged, perform the empowerment of the *mūlamantra* followed by an additional empowerment of three syllables. Recite the words of praise, the seal of offering (*pūjāmudrā*), and the words of recitation twenty-one times as before. For the *argha*, the *namo*, and so forth, the dissolution of the boundary requires only one recitation; dissolve it by circling to the left. Recite the words of the seal of liberation (*vimokṣamudrā*). Perform the heart seals (*hṛdayamudrā*) of the first three families, completing the count as before.
On the third day of the tenth month of the third year of Tenmei (1783),
the year of Bingwu, this was completed at Jōmyō-ji Temple in Ninna-ji,
having been transcribed from the original copy preserved in the Hōkudō repository of Kujū-san.
On the sixth day of the eighth month in the autumn of the *kinkō* year (1321),
the first year of the *Jōwa* era, by a monk of Chikaku-in named Jinin from Tōtōmi.
I sought out the original manuscript and transcribed it.
As for these phonetic glosses (*yinyì*),
they are the phonological explanations provided by a person from Wéihé.
Consequently, its phonetic transcriptions (*fanqie*) and so forth are difficult to reconcile,
and errors such as confusing "Lu" for "Yu" are not few.
I have now collated and corrected the national characters (*guozì*) and engraved them upon woodblocks to ensure their longevity.
At that time, in the tenth month of winter in the same year,
Kaidō of Sōji-in at Fukushū Seizan in Wajō completed the collation of one volume. Jishun.
